# On the Strange Gift of Noticing

I've been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the margins—in the spaces between the big moments we're supposedly supposed to be paying attention to. There's something almost subversive about noticing the small things. It feels like a quiet rebellion against the pressure to always be aiming somewhere, always becoming someone better, always moving forward toward the next checkpoint.

Last week I watched someone at a coffee shop stir their drink for what must have been thirty seconds, just round and round, staring at the coffee swirling. I wondered what they were thinking about. Were they lost in thought, or was stirring just something their hands needed to do while their mind was elsewhere? That moment probably meant nothing to them. They'll never think about it again. But I kept it, somehow. It's still with me.

I think this is what writers and artists mean when they talk about paying attention. Not the kind of attention that's strategic—noticing what will help you get ahead, what will make you more interesting or successful. But the kind that's almost useless. The kind that notices a particular way light falls across someone's face, or the specific rhythm of a stranger's footsteps, or how a particular word sounds funny if you say it five times in a row. The kind of attention that serves no purpose except to make you feel alive.

There's a peculiar comfort in this. In a world that constantly demands we be productive, optimized, always scaling, there's something radical about noticing things that have zero practical value. My observation of the coffee stirrer will never increase my productivity or help me achieve my goals. It won't make me money or improve my relationships or help me live longer. It's just there, a small strange gem I picked up and put in my mental pocket.

I wonder if this is why people keep journals, or take photographs of their breakfast, or write long emails about nothing in particular. We're trying to catch something. We're trying to preserve these moments that don't matter in any rational sense but matter desperately in some other way. We're trying to say: I was here, I noticed this, it was real.

The older I get, the more I understand that most of life is not the major events. It's not the graduation or the wedding or the promotion or the breakup. Those moments get the attention—they're underlined, bolded, marked as Important. But the texture of life, the actual substance of what it feels like to be alive, that's in the other stuff. It's in the Tuesday afternoon when nothing happens. It's in the conversation that wanders without getting anywhere. It's in the way someone laughs at a dumb joke. It's in the particular temperature of the light in winter.

I've also been thinking about how much we're trained not to notice. How we're encouraged to develop tunnel vision, to focus on goals and metrics and outcomes. How the culture of productivity and self-improvement almost necessarily requires us to treat most of experience as irrelevant background noise. You can't simultaneously be constantly optimizing yourself and be genuinely present with what's in front of you. Those two things are fundamentally incompatible.

Maybe that's why people complain about their lives feeling hollow, even when everything on paper looks good. Maybe it's because they haven't genuinely noticed anything in months. They've been too busy becoming the person they thought they needed to be to actually experience the life they're living.

I'm not saying we should all quit our jobs and become wandering monks of observation (though I admit the fantasy appeals to me). I'm just thinking about what happens if we give ourselves permission to notice more. What if noticing was enough? What if it was okay to sit with something beautiful or strange without immediately figuring out how to use it?

There's a Japanese concept called "ma"—the space between things. It's often translated as emptiness or void, but more accurately it refers to the meaningful space, the negative space that gives shape to positive space. I think that's what noticing is. It's the ability to see the ma in life, the spaces between events, the context that gives meaning to the foreground. And paradoxically, learning to see those spaces clearly might be the most meaningful thing we can do.

I read somewhere that the writer Ocean Vuong said something like: beauty is not a luxury, it's a necessity. And I think noticing is similar. The ability to pause and really look at something—really see it—that's not a luxury either. That's how we remember we're human. That's how we make meaning.

There's also something deeply connecting about noticing, I think. When I really observe another person, when I'm genuinely present with their existence, something shifts. The distance between self and other collapses a little bit. I can't hate someone I've really noticed. I can't dismiss them or treat them as invisible when I've actually seen them.

So maybe the project is this: to practice noticing. Not as a way to self-improve or become more interesting or more present (though maybe those would be side effects). But just as an end in itself. To collect small moments. To let your mind wander. To notice the coffee stirrer. To see the light. To hear the actual sound of your own breathing.

In a world that's increasingly virtual, abstract, removed from sensory reality, there's something almost revolutionary about insisting on paying attention to the actual texture of being alive. Not for a purpose. Not to get anywhere. Just to be more alive while you're alive.

That seems important, somehow. Even if I can't quite explain why.
